migration_summary: A self-contained idempotency pattern for applying DDL from a single growing SQL file: a plpgsql apply_migration(name, ddl) function takes an EXCLUSIVE lock on its own bookkeeping table, checks whether a migration with that name has already been recorded, and if not, executes the DDL and records it in the same statement's transaction — so re-running the whole file is always safe. Real, verbatim content (the function definition and its own documented usage example) from the repo's single migrations.sql file.
schema_summary: Generic 'things' table used in the project's own documented usage example; the pattern itself is schema-agnostic.

risk_flags.message: The documented example combines an additive ADD COLUMN with a same-migration ALTER COLUMN ... SET NOT NULL on an existing column in one apply_migration call; if the table already has rows and the new column has no default, the whole multi-statement DDL block fails atomically rather than partially applying.

risk_narrative: The safety property this tool actually provides is re-run idempotency, not migration safety in the row-count sense: EXCLUSIVE-locking the bookkeeping table serializes concurrent apply attempts (so two deploys racing to run migrations.sql can't both apply the same migration), and recording success only after the DDL runs means a killed process leaves the migration unrecorded and safely re-runnable, not half-applied-and-silently-skipped. The tool explicitly documents that 'all statements will be run in a transaction' for a single migration block, which is a real, useful guarantee (all-or-nothing per named migration) but does not make the underlying DDL itself any cheaper or safer against locking/backfill cost.
lessons_learned: Idempotent-application tooling (safe to re-run the whole migration file) and migration-safety tooling (safe against long locks and backfill cost on large tables) are two different problems — this pattern solves the first one well via a locked bookkeeping table and doesn't attempt to solve the second. Don't conflate 'this migration runner is safe to re-run' with 'this specific migration is safe to run on a large table'.
surprise_notes: The EXCLUSIVE lock is on the bookkeeping table (applied_migrations), not on the tables being migrated — it prevents two concurrent deploys from double-applying the same migration, but provides no protection against the DDL itself blocking on unrelated concurrent activity against the target table.

prediction_summary.risk_explanation: Bookkeeping overhead is negligible; actual cost depends entirely on the wrapped DDL, which in the documented example includes a same-migration SET NOT NULL that assumes no NULLs already exist.

dimension_details.note: Real content (function definition + documented usage example) from purcell/postgresql-migrations' single migrations.sql file; the example migrations in that file are commented-out templates illustrating usage, not an executed migration history, and are represented here as such.
